text: A ring of bubbles the size of a copper coin rises through the lake-water around the willow's submerged trunk, breaks the surface, and is gone. Under the sound you cannot quite hear there is another sound — the shape a small bell makes when it has been struck, except this one is not struck. The willow's leaves do not move. Neither do you, for a breath.

Baixu's west sill holds a brown tea-bowl in a dish of river-pebbles. No one is pouring into it; no one has for a long time. As you pass it now, the bowl rings once — a single low chime, the way brass does when the room's temperature has fallen by a single degree. Baixu, if he is here, does not turn to look. If he is not, the pavilion listens with you.

For a breath and a half the gale — which has not stopped since Cloudroot Pass — simply holds. In the pause every pebble, every loose flake of mica on the white stone, sits absolutely still. You feel the wind waiting for a question it has been asked before. Then the gale resumes, louder, as if making up what it had withheld.

In the altar's wind-scoured depression, a palm-sized river pebble sits among the nine incense stubs. It has not moved in forty years. As you pass, a thin fog of breath rises from its surface and curls once, like a finger beckoning, before the wind takes it. The stone is warm.
